checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: A payment balance must survive cache failure and reads may tolerate one cache miss after an update. Which default write path is safer?

options.label: Write behind through the cache
options.sub: acknowledge now and flush to the database later
options.verdict: Write-behind improves throughput, but an acknowledged balance update can disappear if the cache or its write buffer fails before the database flush. That is the wrong durability tradeoff for money.

options.label: Database first, then invalidate
options.sub: commit the source of truth and delete the cached value
options.verdict: The durable database commits first. Invalidating the cache makes the next read miss and repopulate from the source of truth, avoiding acknowledged writes that exist only in cache.

defend.prompt: Which consequences should the design explicitly handle?

options.label: A cache miss is slower because it also queries the database
Concurrent misses for one hot key need single-flight protection
TTL jitter can prevent many keys expiring together
Deleting the cache before the database commit guarantees fresh reads

defend.explain: Cache-aside keeps the database authoritative, but misses pay both cache and database latency. Request coalescing prevents a popular expired key from creating a thundering herd, while jitter spreads unrelated expirations. Commit the database before invalidating so readers do not refill the old database value during the write.

checkpoints.title: Cache reasoning ladder
checkpoints.prompt: Reason from hit rate, eviction, and expiry behavior.

rungs.q: A service handles 100,000 reads/s at a 95% cache hit rate. About how many reads/s reach the database?
rungs.note: The 5% miss path reaches the database: 100,000 × 0.05 = 5,000 reads/s.

rungs.q: Which eviction policy considers both frequency and recency?
rungs.note: LFU favors frequently accessed keys and commonly uses recency to break ties or age old popularity.

rungs.q: What is the primary purpose of adding random jitter to TTL values?
rungs.note: Jitter prevents a large cohort of keys from expiring at the same instant and overwhelming the backing store.

checkpoints.explain: Cache capacity is not just bytes. Hit rate controls backing-store load, eviction controls which working set survives, and expiration shape controls whether misses arrive smoothly or as an avalanche.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.prompt: Build the cache-aside miss path in execution order.
checkpoints.explain: In cache-aside, the application owns both reads. It checks the cache first, queries the database only on a miss, then stores the fresh value with a bounded TTL before responding. Under heavy concurrency, wrap the database-and-fill portion in single-flight coordination so one miss rebuilds the key.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: At exactly 12:00, read latency and database CPU spike although traffic is flat. Which signal identifies the root cause?
checkpoints.explain: The synchronized jump in misses while request volume stays flat points to a cache avalanche: many keys expired together and pushed their reads to the database. Add TTL jitter, stagger warming, and use single-flight for hot keys. Database CPU is the downstream symptom.

wrong.Request Rate: Traffic is flat, so a demand surge does not explain the sudden amplification at exactly the expiry boundary.
wrong.Database CPU: High database CPU explains latency but is an effect of the miss flood, not the initiating signal.
wrong.Network Errors: The small, steady error rate does not correlate with the sharp latency event.
